That is the state jsMsgGetRequest answers 503/10008 in (nats-server v2.15.1, server/jetstream_api.go:3922 with server/jetstream_cluster.go:1481 isLeaderless, which is meta.Leaderless() once the group is older than lostQuorumInterval = 10 s; server/raft.go:4649 stores hasleader from the same value /jsz reports). The committed wait requires both survivors to name a live leader that is not the killed server, which implies hasleader is true on every server that can answer, so the wait closes exactly that guard.

whatElseWasTried: The meta wait's bound cut to 1 ms and the test run 5 times: all 5 passed, because `within` calls its check once before it tests the bound and in those 5 runs the new meta leader was already named 2 ms after the stream election (/legion/scratch/tmp/infra961-tester/m2-wait-1ms.log). An instrumented run of 8 more measured the wait's own duration as 1-2 ms in all 8 (/legion/scratch/tmp/infra961-tester/m2b-waitprobe.log). The wait is therefore a no-op in most runs and blocks in a minority: 8 of the 20 acceptance runs, up to 3.404 s. That is the expected shape for two independent 4-9 s Raft election timers, not a defect.

js.GetMsg polled from the kill until the survivors named a live meta leader, 6 runs: 'context deadline exceeded' from about 0.4 s to 2.7-6.3 s after the kill, then 'ok' (/legion/scratch/tmp/infra961-tester/m4-getmsg-window.log). Nobody answers while no stream leader exists; that window is what the pre-existing 15 s stream-leader wait already covers.

js.GetMsg polled in the gap the committed wait closes - after the stream election, while the survivors still named no agreed live meta leader - 10 runs, 3 of which had such a gap: the read answered 'ok' 1211, 596 and 109 times in a row and was never refused (/legion/scratch/tmp/infra961-tester/m6-gap-read.log). The reason is that most of that gap is a survivor still naming the killed server, where hasleader is true and isLeaderless() is false; the genuinely leaderless sub-window is the one the probe above measured at 4.2-6.5 s. So the single-kill 10008 could not be reproduced in this pod, exactly as the implementer reported from its own wait-removed 20-run loop. It is not needed for the verdict: the committed wait's condition implies the guard that produced the CI failure cannot fire, and the leaderless state it waits past was observed on every run.
